sections.title: Tail information and the zero-one law
paragraphs: For a sequence of real random variables $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$, define $$\mathcal T_n=\sigma(X_{n+1},X_{n+2},\ldots),\qquad\mathcal T=\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}\mathcal T_n.$$ The tail sigma algebra contains the events that can be determined from every tail of the sequence.
Theorem (Kolmogorov zero-one law). If the variables $X_n$ are mutually independent, then $\mathcal T$ is trivial: $$A\in\mathcal T\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathbb P(A)\in\{0,1\}.$$

sections.title: Examples unchanged by deleting a finite prefix
paragraphs: The event $$A=\left\{\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N X_i\text{ exists}\right\}$$ is a tail event. For each fixed $n$, $$\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N X_i-\frac1N\sum_{i=n+1}^N X_i=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\longrightarrow0.$$ Thus the existence of the limit can be read from $X_{n+1},X_{n+2},\ldots$ alone, and $A\in\mathcal T_n$ for every $n$.

The lecture also gives a threshold event of the form $$\left\{\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N X_i\le a\right\},$$ for a fixed real threshold $a$. The same vanishing finite-prefix difference proves it is a tail event.

Another example is a monkey typing a fixed word, such as Hamlet, infinitely many times. A change to finitely many letters changes only finitely many potential word occurrences; whether there are infinitely many occurrences is unchanged.
editorial: The handwritten glyph for the threshold in the second example is unclear; $a$ denotes a fixed threshold here. The tail-event assertion holds for every real $a$. For the first example, the assertion holds whether existence means a finite limit or an extended-real limit, provided that meaning is used consistently.

The zero-one law gives a dichotomy, not a choice between zero and one. For independent letters, proving that a particular word appears infinitely often still requires an additional argument to select the probability.

sections.title: Why tail information is independent of itself
paragraphs: Write $\mathcal G_n=\sigma(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ and $\mathcal G_\infty=\sigma(X_1,X_2,\ldots)$. The proof first shows that each finite-prefix sigma algebra is independent of $\mathcal T$, and then extends this independence to $\mathcal G_\infty$.
proof: By mutual independence and the grouping result, $\mathcal G_n$ is independent of $\mathcal T_n$. Because $\mathcal T\subseteq\mathcal T_n$, it is also independent of $\mathcal T$. The grouping result combines the independent coordinate sigma algebras within a prefix or a tail, just as it combines the collections $\mathcal H_{\alpha,\beta}$ within each group $\mathcal G_\alpha$.

The union $\mathcal P=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\mathcal G_n$ is a pi system: any two of its events belong to a common $\mathcal G_n$, which is closed under intersections. If $A\in\mathcal P$, choose $n_0$ with $A\in\mathcal G_{n_0}$. Then for every $B\in\mathcal T$, $$\mathbb P(A\cap B)=\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B).$$ The pi-system extension theorem gives independence of $\sigma(\mathcal P)$ and $\mathcal T$.

We have $\sigma(\mathcal P)=\mathcal G_\infty$. Indeed, every $X_n$ is $\sigma(\mathcal P)$-measurable, since it is $\mathcal G_n$-measurable. Conversely, every $\mathcal G_n$ lies in $\mathcal G_\infty$, so their generated sigma algebra does too.

Finally, $\mathcal T\subseteq\mathcal G_\infty$. Independence of $\mathcal G_\infty$ and $\mathcal T$ therefore makes $\mathcal T$ independent of itself. For $A\in\mathcal T$, $$\mathbb P(A)=\mathbb P(A\cap A)=\mathbb P(A)^2,$$ hence $\mathbb P(A)$ is zero or one.

recall.question: Reconstruct the zero-one proof. Why does independence from every finite prefix imply independence from the sigma algebra generated by the whole sequence?
answer: The increasing union $\mathcal P=\bigcup_n\sigma(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ is a pi system. Every event in $\mathcal P$ belongs to a finite-prefix sigma algebra and is independent of every tail event. Extend independence to $\sigma(\mathcal P)=\sigma(X_1,X_2,\ldots)$. The tail sigma algebra is contained there, so it is independent of itself and $\mathbb P(A)=\mathbb P(A)^2$.
checks: Use mutual independence to separate a finite prefix from its tail.
Show the increasing union is a pi system.
Finish with independence of an event from itself.

sections.title: A general triviality lemma
paragraphs: Lemma. Suppose $(\mathcal G_n)_{n\ge1}$ are sigma algebras with $\mathcal G_n\subseteq\mathcal G_{n+1}$. If $\mathcal H$ is independent of every $\mathcal G_n$ and $$\mathcal H\subseteq\sigma\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}\mathcal G_n\right),$$ then $\mathcal H$ is trivial.
proof: The preceding proof gives the argument: $\bigcup_n\mathcal G_n$ is a pi system independent of $\mathcal H$, so the sigma algebra it generates is independent of $\mathcal H$. Since it contains $\mathcal H$, each $H\in\mathcal H$ is independent of itself. Therefore $\mathbb P(H)=\mathbb P(H)^2$ and $\mathbb P(H)\in\{0,1\}$.

sections.title: Fubini: an integral over a product space
paragraphs: Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mu)$ be the product of the sigma-finite measure spaces $(\Omega_1,\mathcal F_1,\mu_1)$ and $(\Omega_2,\mathcal F_2,\mu_2)$. Suppose $h$ is measurable on $\mathcal F=\mathcal F_1\otimes\mathcal F_2$. The lecture assumes $$\int h^-\,d\mu<\infty\qquad\text{or}\qquad\int h^+\,d\mu<\infty.$$ Then $$\int_{\Omega_1\times\Omega_2}h\,d\mu=\int_{\Omega_1}\left[\int_{\Omega_2}h(x,y)\,\mu_2(dy)\right]\mu_1(dx).$$ Interchanging the two factor spaces gives the other integration order.
editorial: For $h\ge0$, the integrals may be infinite and the inner integral is defined for every $x$. For signed $h$, the inner integral is defined almost everywhere under the displayed one-sided hypothesis; choose a measurable value, such as zero, on exceptional sections. The extended integral is then well defined. If $\int|h|\,d\mu<\infty$, the inner integral is finite almost everywhere and both iterated integrals are finite.

Dembo states the usual nonnegative-or-absolutely-integrable version. The one-sided version written in the lecture follows by applying the nonnegative theorem to $h^+$ and $h^-$ and subtracting when at least one resulting total is finite. The proof on the handwritten pages starts with bounded $h$ and finite factor measures; the extension after that argument is written out below.

sections.title: Three goals for the bounded finite-measure proof
paragraphs: First assume $h$ is bounded and both measures $\mu_1,\mu_2$ are finite. We must prove three assertions together: each section $y\mapsto h(x,y)$ is $\mathcal F_2$-measurable; the function $$f_h(x)=\int_{\Omega_2}h(x,y)\,\mu_2(dy)$$ is $\mathcal F_1$-measurable; and $$\int h\,d\mu=\int f_h\,d\mu_1.$$

Let $\mathcal H$ be the class of bounded $\mathcal F$-measurable $h$ satisfying these three assertions. To apply the functional monotone-class theorem, the lecture checks that constants belong to $\mathcal H$, that $\mathcal H$ is a vector space, that it is closed under bounded increasing limits of nonnegative functions, and that it contains indicators of a generating pi system.
editorial: The generating pi system is the family of measurable rectangles. In the finite-measure setting, every bounded section and every bounded $f_h$ is integrable; consequently the linearity calculations below never subtract two infinite quantities.

sections.title: Linearity preserves all three goals
paragraphs: Constant functions satisfy the three assertions, including $1\in\mathcal H$. Let $h_1,h_2\in\mathcal H$, $c_1,c_2\in\mathbb R$, and $h=c_1h_1+c_2h_2$.
proof: For fixed $x$, the section $h(x,\cdot)$ is a linear combination of measurable sections and is therefore measurable. Linearity of integration gives $$f_h(x)=c_1f_{h_1}(x)+c_2f_{h_2}(x),$$ so $f_h$ is measurable.

Using the identities for $h_1$ and $h_2$, $$\begin{aligned}\int f_h\,d\mu_1&=c_1\int f_{h_1}\,d\mu_1+c_2\int f_{h_2}\,d\mu_1\\&=c_1\int h_1\,d\mu+c_2\int h_2\,d\mu=\int h\,d\mu.\end{aligned}$$ Thus $h\in\mathcal H$, and $\mathcal H$ is a vector space.

sections.title: Increasing limits preserve all three goals
paragraphs: Let $0\le h_n\in\mathcal H$ and $h_n\uparrow h$, where the limit $h$ is bounded. We check the same three assertions.
proof: For each fixed $x$, the sections $h_n(x,\cdot)$ increase to $h(x,\cdot)$. An increasing limit of measurable functions is measurable. Monotone convergence in $y$ gives $$f_{h_n}(x)=\int h_n(x,y)\,\mu_2(dy)\uparrow\int h(x,y)\,\mu_2(dy)=f_h(x).$$ Hence $f_h$ is measurable as an increasing limit of measurable functions.

Apply monotone convergence to the outer integral and then to the product-space integral: $$\int f_h\,d\mu_1=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int f_{h_n}\,d\mu_1=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int h_n\,d\mu=\int h\,d\mu.$$ Therefore $h\in\mathcal H$.

sections.title: Rectangles complete the proof and permit extension
paragraphs: It remains to put the indicators of a generating pi system into $\mathcal H$. Let $C=D_1\times D_2$, with $D_i\in\mathcal F_i$, and $h=\mathbf{1}_C$.
proof: For fixed $x$, $$h(x,y)=\mathbf{1}_{D_1}(x)\mathbf{1}_{D_2}(y)=\begin{cases}\mathbf{1}_{D_2}(y),&x\in D_1,\\0,&x\notin D_1.\end{cases}$$ The section is measurable. Its integral is $$f_h(x)=\mathbf{1}_{D_1}(x)\mu_2(D_2),$$ a measurable function of $x$. Finally, $$\int f_h\,d\mu_1=\mu_1(D_1)\mu_2(D_2)=\mu(C)=\int h\,d\mu.$$ Thus $\mathbf{1}_C\in\mathcal H$.
The functional monotone-class theorem now gives all bounded $\mathcal F$-measurable functions in $\mathcal H$. This finishes the bounded finite-measure argument developed on the handwritten pages.
editorial: Extension to a nonnegative function with finite factor measures: apply the bounded result to $h\wedge n$ and use monotone convergence for the sections, the outer integral, and the product integral.

Extension to sigma-finite factors: choose $E_n\uparrow\Omega_1$ and $F_n\uparrow\Omega_2$ with $\mu_1(E_n),\mu_2(F_n)<\infty$. For $h\ge0$, put $h_n=h\mathbf{1}_{E_n\times F_n}$. On $E_n\times F_n$, apply the result for the restricted finite measures; outside $E_n$, extend the section integral by zero. Then $h_n\uparrow h$ and $f_{h_n}\uparrow f_h$, so monotone convergence gives the full identity.

Extension to an absolutely integrable signed function: apply the nonnegative theorem to $h^+$, $h^-$, and $|h|$. The set $$N=\left\{x:\int|h(x,y)|\,\mu_2(dy)=\infty\right\}$$ is measurable and has $\mu_1$-measure zero. On its complement the inner signed integral is the difference of two finite integrals; set it to zero on $N$ to obtain a measurable representative. Subtract the two nonnegative identities.

For the lecture's broader one-sided hypothesis, the same argument uses the exceptional set where the integrable part, $h^-$ or $h^+$, has an infinite section integral. That set is null. Off it the signed section integral is well defined, possibly infinite, and subtracting the two nonnegative identities is legitimate because one total is finite. These extension details supplement the handwritten bounded proof.

recall.question: What three facts must be proved in Fubini, and how does the proof pass from rectangles to an arbitrary nonnegative function on sigma-finite factors?
answer: Prove measurable sections, a measurable section integral $f_h$, and equality of the product integral with $\int f_h\,d\mu_1$. Rectangles satisfy all three by direct computation. Under finite measures, linearity and closure under bounded increasing limits allow the functional monotone-class theorem to reach bounded measurable functions. Truncate $h$ to reach nonnegative functions, restrict to increasing finite-measure rectangles to handle sigma-finite factors, and pass to the limit by monotone convergence.
checks: Keep all three measurability/integration goals together.
For signed functions, mention integrability and exceptional sections.

sections.title: Integrate independent inputs one at a time
paragraphs: Theorem. Let $X,Y$ be independent real random variables with laws $P_X,P_Y$, and let $h:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be Borel. If $\mathbb E[h^-(X,Y)]<\infty$ or $\mathbb E[h^+(X,Y)]<\infty$, then $$\mathbb E[h(X,Y)]=\int_{\mathbb R}\left[\int_{\mathbb R}h(x,y)\,P_Y(dy)\right]P_X(dx).$$ The other integration order is valid as well, with the preceding almost-everywhere interpretation for signed sections.
Proposition. The variables $X,Y$ are independent if and only if $$\mathbb E[f(X)g(Y)]=\mathbb E[f(X)]\mathbb E[g(Y)]$$ for every pair of bounded Borel functions $f,g$.
proof: The law-of-a-function formula and the product-law characterization of independence give $$\mathbb E[h(X,Y)]=\int_{\mathbb R^2}h\,dP_{(X,Y)}=\int_{\mathbb R^2}h\,d(P_X\otimes P_Y).$$ Apply Fubini to obtain the iterated formula.
editorial: The product test is stated without a proof on the page. For independent variables, use $h(x,y)=f(x)g(y)$ in the formula and separate the integrals. Conversely, choose $f=\mathbf{1}_A$ and $g=\mathbf{1}_B$; the resulting identity is the defining factorization for all Borel $A,B$. The forward product identity also holds for nonnegative $f,g$, and for integrable $f(X),g(Y)$, since independence first gives $\mathbb E|f(X)g(Y)|=\mathbb E|f(X)|\mathbb E|g(Y)|<\infty$.

sections.title: Tail integrals from Fubini
paragraphs: Theorem (called integration by parts in the lecture). Let $\ell:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty]$ be Borel and define $$F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}\ell(t)\,dt.$$ For any real random variable $X$, $$\mathbb E[F(X)]=\int_{\mathbb R}\ell(t)\mathbb P(X\ge t)\,dt.$$ All quantities are nonnegative, so infinity is allowed.
In particular, for $X\ge0$, choose $\ell(t)=\mathbf{1}_{(0,\infty)}(t)$ to obtain $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^{\infty}\mathbb P(X\ge t)\,dt.$$
proof: On $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$ put $G(x,t)=\ell(t)\mathbf{1}_{\{t\le x\}}$ and use the product measure $P_X\otimes\lambda$, where $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure. The function $G$ is measurable and nonnegative. Integrating in $t$ first gives $$\int G\,d(P_X\otimes\lambda)=\int_{\mathbb R}\left[\int_{\mathbb R}\ell(t)\mathbf{1}_{\{t\le x\}}\,dt\right]P_X(dx)=\int F(x)\,P_X(dx)=\mathbb E[F(X)].$$

Integrating in $x$ first instead gives $$\int G\,d(P_X\otimes\lambda)=\int_{\mathbb R}\left[\int_{\mathbb R}\ell(t)\mathbf{1}_{\{t\le x\}}\,P_X(dx)\right]dt=\int_{\mathbb R}\ell(t)\mathbb P(X\ge t)\,dt.$$ Equating the two expressions proves the formula.
editorial: The integral is with respect to Lebesgue measure in $t$, so the same formula holds with $\mathbb P(X>t)$. For each fixed $x$, including or excluding the endpoint $t=x$ does not change the integral; nonnegative product integration then gives the same total. The symbol $F$ here denotes the accumulated function of $\ell$, not the CDF of $X$.

sections.title: Convolution as the law of a sum
paragraphs: For finite Borel measures $\mu_1,\mu_2$ on $\mathbb R$, define their convolution by $$ (\mu_1*\mu_2)(A)=\int_{\mathbb R}\mu_1(A-y)\,\mu_2(dy),\qquad A\in\mathcal B_{\mathbb R},$$ where $A-y=\{x:x+y\in A\}$. If $s(x,y)=x+y$, this is the pushforward $$\mu_1*\mu_2=s_*(\mu_1\otimes\mu_2).$$

Corollary. If $\mu_1$ has a nonnegative Borel density $f_1$ with respect to Lebesgue measure, then $\mu_1*\mu_2$ has density $$f(z)=\int_{\mathbb R}f_1(z-y)\,\mu_2(dy).$$ In particular, if $\mu_2$ also has density $f_2$, then $$f(z)=\int_{\mathbb R}f_1(z-y)f_2(y)\,dy.$$
proof: The sum map $s$ is measurable. For every Borel $A$, nonnegative product integration gives $$s_*(\mu_1\otimes\mu_2)(A)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\mathbf{1}_A(x+y)\,(\mu_1\otimes\mu_2)(d(x,y))=\int_{\mathbb R}\mu_1(A-y)\,\mu_2(dy).$$ This proves both measurability of the integrand and that the formula defines a measure.

The density argument on the page computes a half-line. For $t\in\mathbb R$, $$\begin{aligned}(\mu_1*\mu_2)(({-\infty},t])&=\int_{\mathbb R}\left[\int_{-\infty}^{t-y}f_1(x)\,dx\right]\mu_2(dy)\\&=\int_{\mathbb R}\left[\int_{-\infty}^{t}f_1(z-y)\,dz\right]\mu_2(dy).\end{aligned}$$ The second line is the translation $z=x+y$.

Since the integrand is nonnegative, Fubini gives $$ (\mu_1*\mu_2)(({-\infty},t])=\int_{-\infty}^{t}\left[\int_{\mathbb R}f_1(z-y)\,\mu_2(dy)\right]dz=\int_{-\infty}^{t}f(z)\,dz.$$ Thus the convolution has the asserted density.
editorial: The first line of the handwritten definition says measures without a finiteness qualification; the density corollary explicitly assumes finite measures. The edited statement keeps finite measures throughout this argument, so product integration and identification by half-lines apply without additional hypotheses. The kernel/pushforward formula also extends to sigma-finite Borel factors; its pushforward need not be sigma finite.

The function $z\mapsto f(z)$ is measurable by nonnegative product integration, and $\int f(z)\,dz=\mu_1(\mathbb R)\mu_2(\mathbb R)<\infty$. Consequently $f$ is finite almost everywhere; on a null set it may be replaced by zero to obtain an everywhere finite representative. Agreement on half-lines determines the finite measure, completing the step from the displayed calculation to a density on all Borel sets.

For independent $X,Y$, their joint law is $P_X\otimes P_Y$ and the sum is the composition with $s$, so $P_{X+Y}=P_X*P_Y$. This connects the convolution definition with the independent-variable discussion.

recall.question: Why is the law of an independent sum a convolution? Derive its density when only the first summand has a density.
answer: Independence gives $P_{(X,Y)}=P_X\otimes P_Y$. Push this law forward through $(x,y)\mapsto x+y$ to get $P_{X+Y}=P_X*P_Y$. If $P_X(dx)=f_X(x)\,dx$, then $$P(X+Y\le t)=\int_{\mathbb R}\int_{-\infty}^{t}f_X(z-y)\,dz\,P_Y(dy)=\int_{-\infty}^{t}\left[\int_{\mathbb R}f_X(z-y)\,P_Y(dy)\right]dz.$$ The bracket is a density of the sum.
checks: Use independence to identify the joint law.
Recognize the bracket as a density.
